A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their complete main texts, appendices, equations, figures, and tables are readable and support comparison despite substantial changes in theoretical scope.

before.justification: Section 5 reports original synthetic convergence and language-modeling results. Appendix F reports original domain-generalization experiments.

after.justification: Section 5 retains original synthetic and real-data results and adds linear-router comparisons. Appendix F reports additional synthetic experiments.

M1.justification: The main regression models replace sparse TopK selection with dense softmax weighting over all experts: compare v1 Equations 2 and 9 with v2 Equations 2 and 8. This changes the model output procedure. The norm perturbation and least-squares objective remain, while real-data implementations still use sparse routing.

E1.justification: Appendix F adds synthetic coverage using linear-router-generated data, creating misspecified settings for cosine models with ReLU or quadratic experts. This is a limited expansion within synthetic regression. All three language corpora and five DomainBed datasets were already evaluated in v1.

E2.justification: v2 adds the conventional linear router to the domain-generalization comparisons in Tables 3-5 and evaluates it against the perturbed router in Appendix F.2. This introduces an important comparison family absent from v1's empirical evaluations. Language-modeling comparators remain unchanged despite replacing the XMoE row labels.

E3.justification: Section 5.1 replaces the stated top-2 data generator and top-4 over-specified fitting with dense mixtures, specifies ReLU instead of ReLU or identity, and uses revised Voronoi losses. Appendix F additionally introduces shared-data comparisons and quadratic experts. These are reported protocol changes; the identical Figure 1 plots do not establish that experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Appendix F.1 tests cosine and perturbed routers on the same linear-router-generated data, directly examining misspecification. Appendix F.2 tests the predicted advantage over linear routing with quadratic experts. These add substantive controlled analyses beyond v1's well-specified simulations; the existing domain-generalization analysis is retained.

E5.justification: Both versions report 20 experiments per synthetic sample size, means with two-standard-deviation error bars, and three-run averages for language modeling and domain generalization. Appendix F follows the existing reporting practice. No new seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported.

E6.justification: New Figure 2 reports convergence rates n^-0.45 versus n^-0.10 for perturbed versus cosine routing, and n^-0.47 versus n^-0.13 for perturbed versus linear routing. Tables 3-5 add linear-router scores, and Table 3 adds cross-dataset averages. Existing language and cosine-router domain scores remain unchanged. v2 also removes v1's erroneous 0.15-0.20 BPC reduction statement.

T1.justification: Voronoi losses change from maxima over selected expert subsets to sums across the full mixture. v1's Proposition 1 on required activated-expert counts and its routing-region stability lemma are removed, with corresponding proof revisions. Appendix B.1 revises the covering argument, and C.1 replaces a detailed proof with an analogy. Exact-specified results are retained and relocated.

C1.justification: The title, abstract, and formal setup recast the contribution from sparse top-K MoE to MoE analyzed without top-K selection. This materially changes the scope of the advertised guarantees. The central claim of slow cosine-router estimation and polynomial improvement through perturbation remains.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly connects expert-estimation rates to expert specialization, contrasts its first-derivative parameter interaction with earlier second-derivative interactions, and interprets Appendix F as support under misspecification. The existing limitations concerning well-specified data and pointwise rather than uniform rates remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Appendix E.2 newly specifies 16 experts, top-2 gating, and an eight-dimensional routing embedding for language modeling. It also corrects the medium-model description from 36 parameters to 36 million. These clarify existing experiments; hardware, training budgets, and reported training times are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds language-modeling and expert-specialization references, including Bengio, Graves, Jelinek, and Krishnamurthy, while removing works on temperature, Gaussian gating, and top-K sparse gating. Related discussion places greater emphasis on specialization and linear-versus-cosine sample efficiency without replacing the central research positioning.

P1.justification: Exact-specified cosine analysis moves from Section 2.1 to Appendix A.1, domain generalization moves from Appendix F to Section 5.3, and Appendix F becomes additional synthetic experiments. The introduction, practical implications, language-modeling explanations, and proof background are also substantially reorganized or expanded.

P2.justification: v2 adds the theoretical-rate summary Table 1 and two-panel Figure 2, moves three domain-generalization tables into the main text, and restructures tables with linear-router rows and an average column. The language table is reformatted. Figure 1 retains its plots but revises its caption, leaving the loss labels inconsistent with the axes.

improvement.justification: New linear baselines, shared-data experiments, and routing details strengthen evaluation and reproducibility. However, v2 replaces sparse analysis with dense analysis while retaining top-2 applications, and changes Figure 1's stated generator and losses without changing its plots; the revised caption also conflicts with its axes. These unresolved connections between theory, settings, and evidence prevent a reliable net quality judgment.
